The August disaster “was not just a local tragedy. It was a warning to the world. And I ask you today: Have you really heard that warning?” Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said at the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday night. “Nearly three years ago, standing in the shadow of our Mount Everest, the secretary-general of the United Nations warned about humanity about the madness and impending climate disaster.”

“That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard enough,” Shah said. “We in Nepal heard it. Our communities heard it. Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it with evidence. But we, the political leaders, have been negligent to translate those warnings in action at the speed and scale that the vulnerable people require.”

International scientists have connected melting permafrost from climate change — caused by burning coal, oil and gas — to the instability of the glacier, which partly collapsed and triggered a massive flood that has killed at least 1,400 people, with even more still missing.

Video above: Powerful video shows woman and two children narrowly escaping Nepal flash flooding

Shah said that Nepal contributed less than one-tenth of 1% of the heat-trapping gases behind climate change. About 99% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and many workers were trapped in tunnels by the flooding.

“We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” said Shah, 36, a former rapper and engineer who is the youngest head of government to address the General Assembly this year. “Our glaciers are retreating, our mountain slopes are becoming unstable, our rivers are becoming less predictable, and every major disaster threatens to erase years of development.”

'Bigger shocks are on the way': The world is inching toward catastrophic climate events

He said climate change ‘does not recognize borders’

In a black Dhaka topi, a traditional brimless Nepali hat, Shah spoke while wearing his signature dark sunglasses, which he uses for medical reasons. He said “the tragic consequences of a warming climate” tell the world that “climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports.”

Subeksha Khadka, a humanitarian and former Miss Nepal International, in an online interview, praised Shah's speech and echoed the warning: "This time Nepal has been on the target, but it could be anyone. This is our story right now, and it can be anybody else’s tomorrow. So it’s time to act.”

Shah did not ask for a specific amount in aid, but he called the international financial aid system inadequate and too bureaucratic. This included a loss and damage fund agreed upon a few years ago for poor nations hit by climate disasters not of their own making.

“Climate finance must not become another bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years” maneuvering when they need help. “When the house is burning, we do not ask a family to complete 50 forms. We act. This is what climate justice means.”

Video above: 2 trapped workers are rescued alive in Nepal

He exhorted the General Assembly to act on relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction — which are traditional international help concepts — but also “responsibility, reparation, resilience.” Reparation is a word and an issue that rankles industrial Western nations like the United States, which is historically the world's biggest carbon emitter.

Climate change made deadly Nepal glacier and rock collapse more likely, according to analysis

He says it's ‘not an isolated disaster’

Over the past 75 years, the United States has spewed about 1,500 times more carbon into the air than Nepal has, according to the Global Carbon Project, a group of scientists that tracks greenhouse gas emissions by countries. Historical emissions matter because carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere for more than a century, trapping heat.

The U.S. this week announced $31 million in aid to Nepal for flood recovery, which brings America's total financial help up to $36 million. It's less than 1% of what Nepal needs.

“Preliminary assessments indicate that from recent disaster alone, Nepal has suffered loss of over $5 billion, nearly 15% of our GDP and a third of our annual budget," Shisir Khanal, Nepal's foreign minister, said Wednesday at the UN climate summit. "Thus, for Nepal, this catastrophe is not merely a humanitarian emergency. It is a development emergency dismantling years of progress. It is a justice crisis exposing the inequities of global climate action, and it is an existential crisis striking at the very survival of our communities and our future.”

Video above: Flash flooding tears through Nepal after glacier triggers massive flood

“What happened in Nepal is not an isolated disaster but a preview of what awaits many vulnerable nations,” Khanal said.

Former United States Vice President Al Gore said in an interview that Nepal's disaster shows that the climate crisis “was getting worse much faster” than people can handle and foreshadows problems with melting glaciers that feed all of the great rivers of Asia, putting the water supply of 2 billion people at risk.

___

Delgado reported from New York. Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed to this report.

title: Ask Nepal, Bangladesh, India: Balen Shah talks of a broken system in UN speech - India Today
description: Ask Nepal, Bangladesh, India: Balen Shah talks of a broken system in UN speech  India Today
publisher.title: India Today
full_article:
"We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food." This was what the Prime Minister of Nepal, Balenendra Shah (better known as Balen Shah) had to say to the world during his maiden address at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City.

In his address on Thursday (September 24), the 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician called for the establishment of a Himalayan climate resilience system, led collectively by India, China and Nepal. Balen made the call after Nepal was hit by the devastating Bhotekoshi floods on August 26, which killed more than 1,400 people and left over 6,000 still missing.

advertisement ❮❯

Read Full Story

Speaking to delegates around the world, the prime minister of Nepal, who is the youngest governing head to speak at the UNGA this year, used the platform to warn the world about the dangers of climate change. He also spoke about the Herculean effort Nepal faces as it struggles to rebuild after the floods that devastated the country's towns and villages in northern and central Nepal on August 26.

Balen's address focused mostly on the need for the nations of the world to work together to mitigate the dangers of climate change and support countries most at risk. But he also had another message to the envoys and the heads of state from across the world who had congregated in New York City.

As the Nepal PM put it, the world had fostered a "broken" order of global cooperation, where "rifles and ammunition cross borders", but fertiliser and fuel "cannot [be] procured at time[s] of need".

He argued that this was not merely Nepal’s "private misfortune", but a wider regional problem affecting countries including Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

"...This is not Nepal's private misfortune. Ask Bangladesh. Ask Bhutan. Ask India. Ask the Maldives. Ask Pakistan. Ask Sri Lanka. Ask any other country in our region and you will hear the same account," he said.

WHAT IS THE BROKEN GLOBAL ORDER THAT BALEN SHAH SPOKE ABOUT AT THE UNGA?

At the heart of PM Balen's argument at the UNGA was a criticism of what he called a "broken" global system where weapons and other military supplies can be moved across the world in a smooth and efficient manner, whereas essential supplies remain difficult to procure, especially for under-developed and developing countries.

Citing Nepal's experiences, the 36-year-old prime minister described how global supply disruptions were impacting ordinary people.

"When a poor farmer in Nepal went to sow her seeds this monsoon, fertilisers didn’t reach her on time," he said, adding, "When we wanted to pave a new highway, there was no bitumen. When the family sat down for an evening meal, there was a shortage of cooking fuel."

PM Balen linked these shortages to a wider combination of climate change and disruptions to global supply chains that Kathmandu could do little to influence.

advertisement

"On the one hand, there are melting glaciers and failing harvests to floods arriving without warning. On the other hand, a global supply chain punishes poor people for causes beyond reason," he stated.

Balen then contrasted the glacial pace of the movement of essential commodities to the rapid speed at which military equipment can cross borders.

"Inter-continental missiles arrive on time. Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear every bottleneck, meet every deadline," he said, adding, "But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure his fertiliser or fuel at market price at a time of need."

The rapper-turned-politician described the existing global system as one where people had "built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food".

In addition, the Nepalese PM said that this is not a situation being faced by Nepal alone. "And this is not Nepal’s private misfortune," Balen stated. He then named Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Pakistan and Sri Lanka as countries being "hit by the climate we did not warm, and hit again by the wars we did not start."

This, according to Balen, shows that "there is a lot more broken than meets the eye in the present order of global cooperation".

advertisement

He concluded by saying that countries, rich or poor, strong and weak, should be able to obtain its necessities as and when needed.

"A country that is willing to pay should be able to buy," Shah stated, adding that a world capable of delivering a weapon anywhere "in seventy-two hours" should have no justification for leaving a farmer without the means to earn "a decent livelihood".

The sight of Balen Shah, who is not known for speaking in public as PM, being able to articulate his points in such a manner in front from envoys from around the world, came as a pleasant suprise to many.

As the environmentalist and climate activist, Ananda Nepali put it in a post on X, "Could someone who rarely gives speeches really present their views so clearly on such a grand international platform? That question was probably in the minds of many Nepalis like me. I was quite excited to hear his address. And when I finally got to hear it, my heart truly swelled with pride."

He added, "The Honourable Prime Minister Balendra Shah today presented Nepal's voice to the world at the United Nations General Assembly in an extremely simple, clear, and confident manner . . . I am proud from the bottom of my heart."

advertisement

In any case, Balen Shah's address, about a broken world order, makes a very important point, especially when one has a look at the series of events happening around the world.

Take for instance, the ongoing US-Iran war. On one hand, the Americans are able to take air defence missiles manufactured in Arkansas and transport them to a desert in Saudi Arabia in a matter of days.

Yet, at the same time, because of the disruptions created by the war, farmers in Nepal have to queue up for long hours to obtain one sack of fertiliser, while people in Bangladesh go for hours without electricity because a power plant ran out of natural gas, that is unable to leave a port in Qatar.

Hence, as Balen pointed out, the global order needs some serious course correction.

ON 24 SEPTEMBER 2026, Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, stood before the United Nations General Assembly in New York and spoke of the “death and destruction of epic proportion” caused by the August flash flood on the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli Rivers in northern Nepal. The flood killed at least 1400 people, with over 6000 still missing. Shah noted that Nepal produces less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet the disaster – with global warming a factor contributing to it – has forced “a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause.”

Shah also had sharp words for the United Nations Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, created in 2022 to respond to the impacts of climate change. He called this fund, and other climate crisis-related finance mechanisms, “grossly inadequate”, and called for a system of grant-based support for affected countries and communities rather than mega loans or a patchwork of small grants. “When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete 50 forms,” he said. “We act. This is what climate justice must mean.”

Shah put Nepal’s needs for physical recovery from the disaster at about 10 percent of the country’s annual GDP. Nepal’s ministry of foreign affairs has placed total reconstruction needs at roughly USD 4.78 billion, including USD 57.67 million for immediate recovery in the first six months. These figures come from a Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) conducted by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and the National Planning Commission, which drew on satellite imagery, drone surveys and data from sector ministries rather than a full on-ground survey. Arjun Bhandari, who led the work on the report, told The Kathmandu Post that the final Post Disaster Needs Assessment now being prepared “could find a variation of around 20 to 30 percent to this figure.”

title: Nepal PM urges climate justice after ‘Himalayan tsunami’ devastates country - UN News
description: Nepal PM urges climate justice after ‘Himalayan tsunami’ devastates country  UN News

full_article:
Addressing the general debate of the Assembly’s 81st session, Mr. Shah said the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster four weeks earlier in northern Nepal had swept through mountain communities with a ferocity described as a “Himalayan Tsunami”.

More than 6,000 people remain missing and damage is estimated at around 10 per cent of Nepal’s gross domestic product (GDP).

“The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world,” he said. “And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?”

Climate justice

Mr. Shah said a warming climate was destabilizing the Himalayan ecosystem, with melting permafrost contributing to unstable mountain slopes and increasing the risks of avalanches, floods and landslides.

The devastation, he added, extended across Nepal’s border with China and downstream towards India.

“Climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports.”

Nepal contributes less than 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse-gas (GHG) emissions, he said, yet disasters repeatedly destroy infrastructure and livelihoods and force the country to borrow to rebuild.

“Climate Justice cannot just remain a beautiful phrase in a United Nations document,” he said.

The Prime Minister proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China to share satellite data and expertise, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, strengthen early-warning systems and coordinate cross-border disaster assistance.

He also called for greater grant-based climate financing, arguing that the Loss and Damage Fund, Global Environment Facility and other mechanisms remain “grossly inadequate”.

“When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete fifty forms. We act,” he said.

Broken logistics for food

Broadening his address, Mr. Shah noted that climate vulnerability was exposing deeper inequalities in the international system, where poorer countries face disruptions caused by conflicts and decisions beyond their control.

He contrasted shortages of fertilizer, fuel and road-building materials in Nepal with the speed at which weapons move around the world.

“We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food,” he said.

Countries like Nepal face a similar predicament, he added: “hit by the climate we did not warm and hit again by the wars we did not start.”

Yet Mr. Shah said those failures strengthened rather than diminished Nepal’s commitment to multilateralism.

“This is why we continue to believe in multilateralism,” he said. “This is why we need a United Nations in which the presence of small poor countries is felt, and we can work together towards just outcomes.”

A new generation

Mr. Shah also linked his international message to political change at home, saying Nepal had arrived at the General Assembly with a renewed democratic mandate reflecting the aspirations of a new generation.

“Our youth have demanded a politics of integrity and accountability,” he said. “This generational shift is not only a national story. It is part of a global awakening against conflicts, inequities, and lack of opportunities.”

Calling for investment in resilience, stronger infrastructure, early-warning systems and reduced dependence on fossil fuels, the Mr. Shah ended by returning to the warning from the Himalayas.

“And when the next warning comes from the rooftop of the world: Let us be ready to hear it, and ready to act.”

full_article:
Nepal’s prime minister and UN chief discussed climate-related vulnerabilities, recovery needs and international support following the devastating Bhote Koshi River disaster.

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah has met United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in New York, with discussions focusing on the recent Bhote Koshi River disaster, climate-related risks and support for affected communities.

Shah, who is in New York to participate in the High-Level Week of the 81st United Nations General Assembly, held talks with Guterres at the United Nations Headquarters at 6:30 PM local time, or 4:15 AM Nepali time on Friday, ahead of his address to the General Assembly, according to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat.

During the meeting, Shah thanked Guterres for his goodwill toward Nepal and congratulated him on his successful tenure. Referring to the significant loss of life and property caused by the disaster along the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa, Shah said the risk of a glacial lake outburst remains high.

Guterres expressed deep condolences over the loss of life and property caused by the Bhote Koshi disaster and said the United Nations stands in solidarity with Nepal on climate-related issues. He also praised the young Nepali delegation.

Recalling his visit to Nepal as a tourist in 1978, Guterres said he remained committed to continuing support for Nepal even after his retirement.

The meeting also covered the rehabilitation of communities living along the river and green reconstruction efforts. The two sides further discussed support for extending the deadline for Nepal’s graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category.

publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah opted out of bilateral meetings on the sidelines of this year’s UN General Assembly in New York. In his stead, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has stepped in to lead Nepal’s diplomatic push in New York, carrying out a broader range of engagements than his predecessor did in the previous gatherings.

At every UN General Assembly, the foreign minister’s contribution tends to get overshadowed by the prime minister, who usually delivers the national statement and handles the bulk of bilateral engagements on the sidelines. Even so, foreign ministers traditionally play a crucial behind-the-scenes role, laying the groundwork for the prime minister’s meetings once they arrive in New York. This year, that dynamic has been upended. Aside from meeting UN Secretary-General António Guterres and brief talks with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Shah did not hold bilateral meetings with any other heads of state or government during his time at the Assembly.

In past years, when Nepali prime ministers travelled to New York for the General Assembly, they would personally take part in a range of groupings—the Group of Least Developed Countries (LDCs), the Group of Landlocked Developing Countries (LLDCs), the UN Economic and Social Council, G77 and China, SAARC and BIMSTEC—along with a full slate of bilateral meetings with counterparts. With Shah largely absent from that circuit this year, much of that duty has been carried out by Khanal.

Since arriving in New York on September 21, Khanal has taken part in roughly 40 meetings—both bilateral and multilateral—in addition to Asia Society events, ceremonies marking the establishment of diplomatic relations between Nepal and other countries, and a range of other programmes. On the sidelines of the Assembly, he has met foreign ministers and senior officials from India, Australia, Poland, Portugal, Japan and the European Union to discuss bilateral relations and cooperation across multilateral forums.

Former chief secretary and foreign secretary Shankar Bairagi commended Khanal's handling of the moment, singling out his interventions on climate change and other pressing issues as particularly strong.

“Foreign ministers who arrive in New York ahead of their prime ministers are always busy. But this time, since the prime minister is not engaged in bilateral meetings and other events, the foreign minister is leading many of those engagements and has become extremely busy,” Bairagi said. “Ministers have to lead several meetings and events and meet their counterparts. This time, the way the foreign minister has addressed various events and conveyed Nepal’s message to the global community has been excellent.”

Foreign Minister Khanal’s agenda has kept the climate focus front and centre. Beyond attending the Assembly’s opening session, Khanal is scheduled to chair a Nepal-organised event titled “Sagarmatha to the Sea: A Call to Action for a Climate-Resilient Future”, which will examine the growing impact of climate change on the Himalayas and its broader consequences, while drawing international attention to the need for stronger climate action.

At a Global South ministerial meeting, Khanal argued that developing countries should have a greater say in shaping international rules and global institutions, rather than simply implementing rules set by others. He has also taken part in ministerial-level meetings of the LDCs, the LLDCs, the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), and the G77 and China.

At a ministerial meeting of the UN Mediation Group, he emphasised dialogue, confidence-building and mediation as tools for conflict prevention and the peaceful resolution of disputes. In another programme, a UNGA-related meeting on the Right to Development, he stressed the importance of political will, international solidarity, technology and concessional financing for developing countries, while flagging the challenges facing progress on the Sustainable Development Goals.

Majeet Dhakal, lead adviser to the Chair of the Least Developed Countries Group on Climate Change, who is also attending multiple events on the sidelines of the Assembly, said Khanal’s handling of Nepal’s agenda had been well received.

“After the prime minister’s statement, a tone has been set in New York, but how we proceed further and sustain this attention is important,” Dhakal said. “The performance of both the prime minister and the foreign minister was well regarded in New York.”

Dhakal said that the Nepali delegation has received increased attention in multiple forums and events.
